walkthrough:
Split the Chloroplast into Two Working Areas**
Think of the chloroplast as having two factories. The background fluid is the stroma and the membrane factory inside it is the thylakoids and grana. Each factory runs one stage of photosynthesis, so linking structure to function means matching each part to its stage.

Stroma for the Calvin Cycle**
The stroma is the aqueous ground substance where the light-independent stage happens. It contains all the Calvin cycle enzymes, including rubisco for carbon fixation. It also holds ribosomes, circular DNA, lipid droplets and starch grains made as product, which lets the chloroplast make some of its own proteins and store product temporarily.

Thylakoid Membranes for the Light-Dependent Stage**
The internal membranes form many fluid-filled sacs called thylakoids, stacked into grana and linked by intergranal lamellae. Stacking gives a very large surface area in a small volume, so many pigment molecules and carriers can be packed in for maximum light absorption and electron transport.

Photosystems to Harvest Light**
Pigments are not scattered randomly. They are grouped in light-harvesting clusters called photosystems. Each has a chlorophyll a primary pigment at the reaction centre surrounded by accessory pigments such as chlorophyll b, carotenes and xanthophylls. Accessory pigments absorb different wavelengths and pass energy to the reaction centre, so more of the spectrum is used.

Membrane Proteins to Make ATP**
Thylakoid membranes also hold electron carriers and ATP synthase. Light excites electrons that flow along carriers, pumping protons into the thylakoid space. Protons then flow back through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis to drive photophosphorylation, directly linking membrane structure to ATP production.

Final answer: Stroma is fluid ground substance site of light-independent stage / Calvin cycle, containing enzymes e.g. rubisco and ribosomes, DNA, starch. Internal membrane system of fluid-filled thylakoids stacked as grana provides large surface area for light-dependent stage. Grana membranes hold photosynthetic pigments in photosystems / light-harvesting clusters with chlorophyll a reaction centre surrounded by accessory pigments that pass energy to centre and absorb different wavelengths for maximum absorption. Membranes hold electron carriers and ATP synthase for photophosphorylation / chemiosmosis.

walkthrough:
Extract a Concentrated Mixture**
You cannot separate pigments while they are still inside cells. Grind fresh leaf with a solvent such as propanone or ethanol to dissolve the hydrophobic pigments and release a mixture of chlorophylls and carotenoids. Gently concentrate the extract so the spots will be dark enough to see after separation.

Set Up the Origin Correctly**
Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of chromatography paper or a TLC plate - pencil is insoluble so it will not move. Spot a small drop of concentrated extract onto the line and let it dry, repeating to build a small concentrated spot. A small spot keeps the final bands sharp.

Run the Chromatogram**
Stand the paper vertically in a covered jar containing a small depth of chromatography solvent, keeping the baseline just above the solvent level so pigments do not dissolve directly into the jar. The solvent rises up the paper by capillarity and carries dissolved pigments with it.

Explain Separation and Identification**
Each pigment has a different solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper, so each travels at a different speed and stops a unique distance up the paper, forming separate coloured bands. Calculate $R_f$ = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front to identify each pigment by comparison with known values. If bands overlap, run two-dimensional chromatography at right angles in a second solvent for better separation.

Final answer: Grind leaf in solvent to extract mixture of pigments and concentrate extract. Draw pencil baseline on chromatography paper / TLC plate and spot concentrated extract on line. Place paper vertically in jar of solvent with baseline above solvent level. Solvent rises by capillarity, carrying pigments at different speeds due to different solubilities / affinities. Pigments separate as they ascend, each travelling a unique distance identified by $R_f$ value. Two-dimensional chromatography at right angles gives better separation.
